also: he doesn’t know what the score is

terms.gloss: what’s the matter? what’s going on?
terms.grammar: negōtī, partitive genitive of negōtium (the older form of negōtiī)
evidence: Plaut. Most. 2.2.27; Plaut. Capt. 3.5.11: quid negōtī est, quamobrem suscēnsēs mihi? (Lewis & Short), s.v. negōtium

terms.gloss: what’s going on? how are things?
evidence: Ter. Ad. 373–374: Hem, Dēmea, haud aspexeram tē. Quid agitur?
terms.comment: In comedy also the greeting “how are things?” (see how are you).

evidence: Plaut. Epid. 203; Plaut. Merc. 964: Quid reī est?
Liv. 3.48.4: quid hoc reī sit (Lewis & Short s.v. percontor)
terms.comment: Plautus’s question, without hīc; with hoc, “what is all this?”.

terms.gloss: what is going on, what is being done
terms.grammar: indirect question with the passive of agō, after scīre, vidēre, nescīre
evidence: Cic. Mur. 83: est tuum, Catō, vidēre quid agātur (Lewis & Short s.v. sum)
Cic. Att. 3.8.2: nunc istīc quid agātur, magnopere timeō (Lewis & Short s.v. timeō)
Traupman 107: he doesn’t know what the score is, nescit quid agātur
terms.comment: “What is being done”: the impersonal passive of agō covers what English calls “what’s happening”. As a direct question, quid agitur?.

phrases.latin: Hem, Dēmea, haud aspexeram tē. Quid agitur?
phrases.english: Oh, Demea, I didn’t see you. How are things?
